Basal metabolic rate measurements for the Starred wood quail (Odontophorus stellatus) were obtained through indirect calorimetry on captive individuals under thermoneutral conditions. The maximum resting oxygen consumption was recorded at 209.09 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 209.09 milliliters of oxygen per hour] when birds were maintained at an ambient temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. This metabolic rate, reflecting the energetic costs of physiological maintenance in a stable thermal environment, aligns closely with values reported for other small-bodied New World quail species inhabiting Neotropical forests. The elevated temperature required to achieve a truly basal measurement underscores the species adaptation to warm, humid understory conditions where thermoregulatory demands are comparatively low.

Reproductive output in the Starred wood quail follows a pattern typical of tropical forest-dwelling galliforms, characterized by modest clutch sizes and extended breeding intervals. Females lay precisely four eggs per clutch [N_R_i = four eggs per clutch], and field observations indicate that a single clutch is produced each year [F_R_i = single clutch is produced each year]. This low annual fecundity is consistent with the life-history strategy observed in the closely related Marbled wood quail (Odontophorus gujanensis), from which these data are primarily drawn. The relatively small number of offspring produced annually is likely linked to the high level of biparental care and the prolonged period of nest attendance required in predator-rich environments, where each reproductive attempt carries substantial energetic and survival costs for the attending adults.

Early developmental stages are brief relative to many other galliform species, though critical details have been inferred from studies of congeneric taxa. Eggs incubated at 38 °C [T = 38 °C] hatch after approximately 26 days [ab = approximately 26 days], a duration characteristic of wood quails and reflecting the rapid embryonic development permitted by stable tropical incubation temperatures. The freshly laid eggs, measuring 38.9 millimeters in length and 27.8 millimeters in width based on Odontophorus gujanensis specimens, are estimated to have an initial wet weight of 15.7 grams [Ww0 = 15.7 grams]. This relatively modest egg mass represents a substantial maternal investment given the small clutch size, with each egg containing sufficient yolk reserves to support the altricial-precocial continuum typical of galliform hatchlings during their first days of life.

Post-hatching development proceeds through a series of clearly defined milestones under the thermal conditions characteristic of the species active metabolic state at 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. The downy chicks achieve their first flight and depart the nest after only 9 days from hatching [tx = 9 days from hatching], an exceptionally rapid fledging period for a bird of this body size that likely serves as an adaptation to high nest predation rates in lowland Amazonian forests at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. Sexual maturity, defined by the onset of gonadal development and reproductive competence, is reached at 80 days after hatching [tp = 80 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C]. However, the time since birth at first successful brood is considerably delayed, occurring at 1.8 years after hatching [tR = 1.8 years after hatching], a postponement that reflects the extended period required for young birds to acquire high-quality territories and establish pair bonds within saturated populations at a temperature of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C].

Adult body mass exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining a maximum recorded weight of 315 grams [Wwi = 315 grams] while males reach a substantially larger final weight of 358 grams [Wwi = 358 grams]. This reversed size dimorphism is unusual among galliforms and may relate to the competitive pressures of male-male competition for breeding territories within dense understory vegetation. Maximum reported longevity in the wild stands at approximately 14.6 years [am = approximately 14.6 years] under the same thermal regime of 40.7 °C [T = 40.7 °C], a lifespan that is notably extended for a bird of this body mass and likely reflects the low extrinsic mortality rates characteristic of stable tropical environments. This combination of modest reproductive output, extended developmental trajectory, and substantial longevity positions the Starred wood quail as a classic slow life-history strategist among Neotropical forest birds.
